lede: Some rows are only identified by two columns together: a SKU is stocked in several warehouses, so the stock level for a shipment needs both. And some matches aren't equalities at all, like a quantity that falls inside a band.
objectives: Join on a key made of several columns with `on=[...]`
See how joining on part of a key multiplies rows
Write join conditions with `&` and ranges with `between`
Choose between a condition in the join and a filter after an outer join

blocks.md: `shipments` lists parcels leaving a warehouse, each with a `warehouse_id` and a `sku`. `inventory` has one row per **warehouse and SKU**: the same packing tape, `SKU-1003`, is stocked in three warehouses. To see the stock a shipment draws on, the match has to use both columns. Watch what happens with only one.

blocks.title: Half a key multiplies rows
blocks.code:
by_sku = shipments.join(inventory, on="sku", how="inner")
print(shipments.count(), "shipments,", by_sku.count(), "rows when joined on sku alone")

by_sku.select(
    "shipment_id",
    shipments["warehouse_id"].alias("ship_from"),
    inventory["warehouse_id"].alias("stock_in"),
    "sku",
    "on_hand",
).orderBy("shipment_id", "stock_in").show()
blocks.note: Each tape shipment matched all three warehouses that stock tape. Nothing errors: the result is just wrong, and any total built on it is three times too big.

blocks.md: Pass a list to `on` to match on several columns at once: a row pairs only when **every** listed column is equal. As with a single key, each listed column appears once in the result.

blocks.title: Join on the whole key
blocks.note: Four shipments, four rows, and each shows the stock of its own warehouse.

blocks.md: `on=[...]` only works when the columns have the same names on both sides. The general form is a condition: equalities joined with `&`, each in its own parentheses, the same way you combine filter conditions. Aliases keep the two sides apart.

blocks.title: The same join as a condition
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

s = shipments.alias("s")
i = inventory.alias("i")

same_place = (F.col("s.warehouse_id") == F.col("i.warehouse_id")) & (F.col("s.sku") == F.col("i.sku"))

s.join(i, same_place, "inner").select("s.shipment_id", "s.warehouse_id", "s.sku", "i.on_hand").orderBy("shipment_id").show()
blocks.note: Same rows as before. With a condition, both copies of the key columns are kept, so name the side you want.

blocks.md: A join condition doesn't have to be an equality. To give each shipment a size band from a small band table, match on a range: `F.col("quantity").between(low, high)` is true when the quantity is at least `low` and at most `high`, both ends included.

blocks.title: Match on a range
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

bands = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("single", 1, 1), ("small", 2, 9), ("bulk", 10, 999)],
    "band STRING, min_qty INT, max_qty INT",
)

with_band = shipments.join(bands, F.col("quantity").between(F.col("min_qty"), F.col("max_qty")), "left")
with_band.select("shipment_id", "quantity", "band").orderBy("shipment_id").show()
blocks.note: Bands must not overlap: a quantity inside two bands would match both and the shipment would appear twice. A left join keeps a shipment whose quantity fits no band, with a NULL band.

blocks.md: With an outer join, **where** a condition goes changes the answer. Put it in the join condition and it only decides which right-side rows match; every left row stays. Put it in a `filter` after the join and it removes left rows too, including those whose right side is NULL.

blocks.title: In the join or after it
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

s = shipments.alias("s")
i = inventory.alias("i")
same_place = (F.col("s.warehouse_id") == F.col("i.warehouse_id")) & (F.col("s.sku") == F.col("i.sku"))

low_stock = same_place & (F.col("i.on_hand") < 300)
s.join(i, low_stock, "left").select("s.shipment_id", "s.sku", "i.on_hand").orderBy("shipment_id").show()

s.join(i, same_place, "left").filter(F.col("i.on_hand") < 300).select("s.shipment_id", "s.sku", "i.on_hand").orderBy("shipment_id").show()
blocks.note: In the join, all four shipments stay and only the low-stock ones get a value: a report of every shipment with a warning column. As a filter, only the two low-stock shipments are left.

concept.prompt: Inventory has one row per warehouse and SKU. A SKU is stocked in 4 warehouses. How many rows does one shipment of that SKU give in `shipments.join(inventory, on="sku")`?
concept.why: Joining on part of the key matches every inventory row with that SKU, one per warehouse. Join on `["warehouse_id", "sku"]` to get one.

choices: It is true for 2 and 9 as well as everything in between
It only works in filter, not in a join condition
concept.why: `between` includes both ends, and like any condition it works in a filter or a join.

concept.prompt: A left join puts `on_hand < 300` in the join condition. What happens to a shipment whose stock is 560?
choices: It is removed from the result
concept.why: In a left join every left row stays. The extra condition only stops that inventory row from matching, so the right-side columns are NULL.

review: When a key is several columns, join on all of them: `on=["warehouse_id", "sku"]`.
Joining on part of a key quietly multiplies rows; check counts before and after a join.
A join condition can combine equalities with `&`, each in its own parentheses.
Conditions can be ranges: `F.col("x").between(low, high)` includes both ends. Ranges must not overlap.
In an outer join, a condition in the join keeps every left row; a filter afterwards removes rows.
